title: Key hierarchy and the HSM
summary: See how envelope encryption keeps a stored secret useless without KMS access.

blocks.text: 1Claw encrypts every secret with envelope encryption. A random 256-bit DEK encrypts the value with AES-256-GCM, then a per-vault KEK that never leaves the HSM wraps the DEK. In production the HSM is Google Cloud KMS at FIPS 140-2 Level 3 protection.

items: JWT signing key: one Ed25519 key per deployment, in the same KMS key ring
KEK: one symmetric key per vault, wraps and unwraps DEKs
DEK: fresh 256-bit key per secret version, never persisted in the clear
KEKs rotate on a 365-day period; KMS keeps old versions for decrypt

blocks.text: Every KMS encrypt, decrypt, and sign includes a CRC32C checksum. If the checksum mismatches in transit, the operation fails immediately instead of returning corrupt data.

steps.text: Exchange your API key for a bearer token. Replace 1ck_your_key_here with your real key from Settings → API Keys.
steps.code:
export ONECLAW_API_KEY="1ck_your_key_here"
export TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST https://api.1claw.co/v1/auth/api-key-token \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"api_key\":\"$ONECLAW_API_KEY\"}" | jq -r .access_token)

steps.text: Use your vault UUID from `1claw vault list` or Foundations.

Store a secret. Use a 1ck_ user key (which has full access), or an agent JWT with a write policy on this path. On the wire this is plaintext; at rest 1Claw generates a DEK, encrypts the value, and wraps the DEK with the vault KEK.

Read the secret back. The API returns the decrypted value; reason about what is stored at rest vs. returned in memory. The database holds only ciphertext, the wrapped DEK, IV, and tag. Without a KMS unwrap none of it decrypts.

blocks.text: You stored a secret and can now explain why a stolen database is worthless: the plaintext DEK exists only in memory during the operation, and the KEK never leaves the HSM.

blocks.situation: An engineer reports that an attacker briefly had shell on an application server. That server does not hold key material; it authenticates to the HSM and calls it to sign and unwrap. Access was revoked after roughly forty minutes.
blocks.question: What is the correct assessment of the damage?

options.text: The keys are safe because they never left the HSM, so no action is needed.
options.feedback: Half right, and the dangerous half is missing. Non-exportability means the attacker could not take the key with them, which is a real containment win. But for forty minutes they could ask the HSM to perform operations, and it would have complied. You have to establish what was signed or decrypted in that window.

options.text: Assume every operation the server could request was performed, audit the HSM log for that window, and rotate anything the results touched.
options.feedback: Correct. An HSM protects against key theft, not key misuse. The key is intact, so you do not need to re-key the hierarchy, but every operation in that window is suspect and the audit log is the only record of what actually happened.

options.text: Rotate the KEK immediately and re-wrap every DEK.
options.feedback: Disproportionate, and it treats the wrong risk. The KEK was never exposed, so rotating it costs real effort and fixes nothing. Rotation is the answer to key compromise; this was credential compromise.

options.text: Destroy the HSM key version so anything signed during the window becomes invalid.
options.feedback: This confuses signing with encryption. Destroying a key version makes data encrypted under it unreadable, but it does not retroactively invalidate signatures already produced and accepted by others. You would also lose access to legitimate data.

quiz.question: What wraps the DEK before it is stored?
options: The per-vault KEK inside the HSM
quiz.explanation: Each vault has one KEK in KMS that wraps and unwraps that vault's DEKs.

quiz.question: What FIPS level is the production HSM?
quiz.explanation: Production KMS keys use HSM protection at FIPS 140-2 Level 3.

quiz.question: How often do KEKs rotate automatically?
quiz.explanation: KEKs rotate on a 365-day period, the NIST SP 800-57 maximum for symmetric KEKs.

title: Customer-managed keys (CMEK)
summary: Add a client-side AES-256-GCM layer so 1Claw stores only your key's fingerprint.

blocks.text: CMEK double-encrypts secrets. You encrypt the value with your own AES-256-GCM key in the browser or your process, then 1Claw applies its HSM envelope encryption on top. Your key never touches the server; only its SHA-256 fingerprint is stored so the vault knows which key was used. CMEK is available on Business and Enterprise plans.
The client-side wire format is one version byte (0x01), a 12-byte IV, the ciphertext, then a 16-byte GCM auth tag. A full server compromise yields only doubly-encrypted blobs.
Requires Business or Enterprise plan.

steps.text: Install the SDK and have an API key ready.
Export your API key and vault ID. Replace with your real values from Settings → API Keys and `1claw vault list`.
Exchange your API key for a bearer token.
Save the code below as `cmek-demo.ts`. It generates a 256-bit key, encrypts a secret, stores it, reads it back, and decrypts it. Store the key safely because you need it for every read and write.
Copy the fingerprint value printed above into the curl body below. Enable CMEK on the vault by sending only the fingerprint.

blocks.text: To rotate, send the old and new keys to POST /v1/vaults/:id/cmek-rotate. The server re-encrypts in batches of 100, atomically per batch, and holds both keys in memory only for the duration of the job.
The vault now requires your key for every value, and 1Claw cannot decrypt your secrets unilaterally.

Two easy mistakes here. generateCmekKey, cmekFingerprint, cmekEncrypt and cmekDecrypt all return promises, so every one needs await. And cmekEncrypt takes (plaintext, key) in that order, both as Uint8Array: swapping them produces a blob that will never decrypt.

blocks.situation: A customer on CMEK reports that their finance team lost the laptop holding the only copy of their key. They have their dashboard login and their secrets are all still listed in the vault.
blocks.question: What can you actually do for them?

options.text: Restore the key from the server-side backup taken at enrolment.
options.feedback: There is no such backup, and that is the point of CMEK. Only the SHA-256 fingerprint is stored server-side, which can verify a key but cannot reconstruct one.

options.text: Nothing recovers the values. The ciphertext is unreadable, and they must re-supply every secret under a new key.
options.feedback: Correct, and it is the trade they accepted. The key never left their device, so the provider genuinely cannot help. This is why CMEK enrolment should be paired with an escrow process the customer controls.

options.text: Use server-assisted rotation to move the secrets onto a new key.
options.feedback: Rotation re-encrypts by decrypting with the old key first. Without that key there is nothing to rotate from. The feature helps you change keys, not recover from losing one.

options.text: Read the values from the audit log, which records secret access.
options.feedback: The audit log records that an access occurred, along with who and when. It never records the value; if it did, it would be a second copy of every secret in a place with weaker controls.

quiz.question: What does 1Claw store about your CMEK key?
options: An encrypted copy in the HSM
quiz.explanation: Only the SHA-256 fingerprint is stored so the vault can track which key was used.

quiz.question: What algorithm does the client-side CMEK layer use?
quiz.explanation: CMEK encrypts values client-side with AES-256-GCM before the HSM layer is applied.

quiz.question: What protects a secret if the CMEK vault's database is stolen?
options: Only the fingerprint is needed to decrypt
It is doubly encrypted and useless without your key
quiz.explanation: Each secret carries two independent encryption layers, so a backup yields only doubly-encrypted blobs.

title: MPC secret storage
summary: Split a secret's DEK across parties so no single holder can reconstruct it.

blocks.text: MPC splits each secret's DEK into shares so one compromised holder cannot decrypt. It layers on top of the standard HSM envelope encryption and is set per vault. The custody mode is immutable once set.

items: 2of2_client_custody: XOR split between the server HSM and you; you hold a client_share
2of3_multi_hsm: Shamir 2-of-3 across GCP, AWS, and Azure; no client share
2of3_client_custody: Shamir 2-of-3 with two HSMs plus your client share

blocks.text: For client-custody modes, store the client_share safely. Lose it on a 2of2_client_custody vault and the secret cannot be recovered, because the server holds only its single share.
Create a dedicated vault for MPC testing; custody mode cannot be changed after it is set.
Requires Pro or higher plan.

steps.text: Export your API key and vault ID. Use your vault UUID from `1claw vault list` or Foundations.
Exchange your API key for a bearer token.
Enable MPC with XOR client custody. This choice is permanent for the vault.
Write a secret. The PUT response includes a base64 client_share you must keep. Capture it from the response.
steps.code:
RESPONSE=$(curl -s -X PUT https://api.1claw.co/v1/vaults/$VAULT_ID/secrets/api-keys/stripe \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"value":"sk_live_abc123","type":"api_key"}')
CLIENT_SHARE=$(echo "$RESPONSE" | jq -r .client_share)
echo "Save this client_share permanently: $CLIENT_SHARE"

steps.text: Read it back by sending your share in X-Client-Share. Without the header the read fails.

blocks.text: The vault now returns a client_share on write and requires it on read, so 1Claw alone cannot reconstruct the DEK.

blocks.situation: You are choosing a custody mode for a vault holding the signing material behind a treasury that moves large sums. The team is small and operationally inexperienced, and there is no formal key-escrow process.
blocks.question: Which mode fits, and why?

options.text: 2of2_client_custody, so the provider mathematically cannot act alone.
options.feedback: The trust property is exactly what you want, but pair it with this team and it is a liability. Both shares are required, one is held by them, and losing it is unrecoverable. Strong cryptography plus weak key operations is how funds get permanently locked, not secured.

options.text: 2of3_multi_hsm, so no single HSM provider holds a complete key and losing one share is survivable.
options.feedback: Correct for this team. It removes single-provider trust, which is the threat that matters here, while tolerating the loss of one share. Client custody is stronger against a colluding provider, but only if the client can actually operate a key.

options.text: No MPC. Standard envelope encryption in the HSM is enough for a treasury.
options.feedback: Defensible for most vaults, but this one concentrates unusual value in a single provider's control. That is precisely the case where splitting custody earns its operational cost.

options.text: 2of3_client_custody, for the strongest guarantee available.
options.feedback: It is the strongest, and it still requires this team to hold and never lose a share. Choosing the maximum guarantee without the operational maturity to support it trades a modest risk for a catastrophic one.

quiz.question: Which mode returns a client_share and needs X-Client-Share on reads?
quiz.explanation: The 2of2_client_custody XOR split gives you a client_share and requires it on every read.

quiz.question: Can a vault's MPC custody mode be changed after it is set?
quiz.explanation: The custody mode is immutable once set on a vault.

quiz.question: Where are the shares stored in 2of3_multi_hsm?
quiz.explanation: 2of3_multi_hsm distributes three Shamir shares across GCP KMS, AWS KMS, and Azure Key Vault.

title: Shroud TEE proxy
summary: Route a chat completion through Shroud so it is inspected inside a hardware TEE.

blocks.text: Shroud is an OpenAI-compatible LLM proxy running inside a confidential GKE node with AMD SEV-SNP. Your agent sends chat completions to Shroud instead of the provider. Shroud authenticates the agent, resolves the provider key, runs threat detection and secret redaction, then forwards the request. Secrets never leave your infrastructure in the clear.

items: Endpoint: POST https://shroud.1claw.co/v1/chat/completions
X-Shroud-Agent-Key: agent_id:api_key (the agent's ocv_ key)
X-Shroud-Provider: openai, anthropic, google, gemini, and others
Secret redaction, PII detection, and prompt-injection scoring run before the model sees the prompt

blocks.text: Prompt injection is scored 0.0 to 1.0. Anything above 0.9 is a hard block regardless of the agent's configured threshold, which defaults to 0.7.

steps.text: Set your agent credentials. Replace with your agent_id from agent creation and your ocv_ key from the agent's settings page.
Quick start: pass your provider key directly via X-Shroud-Api-Key. For production, store the key in the vault at providers/openai/api-key and grant the agent read access instead.
Parse the response. It follows the standard OpenAI shape.
steps.code:
curl -s -X POST https://shroud.1claw.co/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "X-Shroud-Agent-Key: $ONECLAW_AGENT_ID:$ONECLAW_AGENT_API_KEY" \
  -H "X-Shroud-Provider: openai" \
  -H "X-Shroud-Api-Key: sk-your-openai-key" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"gpt-4o-mini","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Hello"}]}' | jq -r '.choices[0].message.content'

blocks.text: No editor supports the X-Shroud headers natively. Run npx @1claw/cli proxy locally to bridge Cursor, Claude Code, and Copilot traffic into Shroud.
Your agent's LLM traffic now flows through the TEE proxy, inspected and redacted, with a normal OpenAI-style response coming back.

blocks.situation: An agent has intents_require_tee set. A developer reports that their new service calls the Intents API directly at api.1claw.co and receives a 403, and asks you to disable the flag so they can ship.
blocks.question: What is the right response?

options.text: Disable intents_require_tee for that agent, since the call is coming from your own infrastructure.
options.feedback: This is the reasoning the flag exists to prevent. The guarantee is not that the caller is trustworthy, it is that signing is routed through an attested enclave. Turning it off because a trusted service is inconvenienced removes the property for every caller, trusted or not.

options.text: Route the service through shroud.1claw.co instead, which is what the flag requires.
options.feedback: Correct. The 403 is the control working as designed. Shroud sets an HMAC-signed X-1Claw-TEE-Origin header that the Vault verifies, so the fix is to send the request through the enclave rather than to remove the requirement.

options.text: Add the service's IP to an allowlist so it can bypass the check.
options.feedback: The check is not about network origin, so an IP allowlist cannot satisfy it. It verifies a shared-secret HMAC header that only Shroud can produce, precisely so that reaching the API from a permitted address is not sufficient.

options.text: Give the service a second agent identity without the flag set.
options.feedback: This is the flag disabled with extra steps, and it is worse: you now have two identities for one workload, one of which quietly lacks the control, and the audit trail no longer tells you which path a signature took.

quiz.question: What is the format of the X-Shroud-Agent-Key header value?
quiz.explanation: The value is exactly agent_id:api_key, with the agent's ocv_ key on the right.

quiz.question: At what prompt-injection score does Shroud hard-block regardless of config?
quiz.explanation: Scores above 0.9 are always blocked, even if the agent's threshold is higher.

quiz.question: What TEE technology runs the Shroud proxy?
quiz.explanation: Shroud runs on GKE confidential nodes using AMD SEV-SNP.

title: Zero trust and the risk engine
summary: Plant a honeytoken canary so any read trips a critical verdict and revokes sessions.

blocks.text: 1Claw assumes no implicit trust. Every request is authenticated, authorized against policy, and audited to a tamper-evident SHA-256 hash chain. Revocation is immediate: delete a policy and access stops on the next request. On top of that, the risk engine scores every authentication event in real time.

items: Geo-velocity: impossible travel between two locations
First-seen: a new ASN, country, or device for this principal
Honeytokens: decoy secrets whose access records a critical verdict
DPoP binds a JWT to a client keypair (RFC 9449)

blocks.text: A critical verdict triggers Continuous Access Evaluation: all of that principal's active tokens are revoked, their JTIs are added to the revoked list, and their next request fails auth. Verdicts carry a 15-minute TTL.

steps.text: Export your API key and vault ID. Use your vault UUID from `1claw vault list` or Foundations.
Exchange your API key for a bearer token.
Create a honeytoken. The honeytoken registers a canary on this path. Any read of this path triggers a critical alert and session revocation. Pick a path that looks valuable so an attacker is tempted.
steps.code:
curl -s -X POST https://api.1claw.co/v1/risk/honeytokens \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"vault_id":"'"$VAULT_ID"'","secret_path":"api-keys/production","notes":"Canary for vault breach"}'

steps.text: Confirm it is armed by listing your honeytokens.
Optional: read the honeytoken path and confirm the token is revoked on the next request.
steps.code:
curl -s https://api.1claw.co/v1/vaults/$VAULT_ID/secrets/api-keys/production \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
# Now try another request; it should fail with 401
curl -s https://api.1claw.co/v1/vaults/$VAULT_ID/secrets/api-keys/production \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

blocks.text: When a honeytoken is read, the current request is not blocked so the attacker is not tipped off. Their next authentication attempt is denied instead.
You now have a live canary: any read of api-keys/production records a critical verdict and revokes that principal's sessions.

blocks.situation: A nightly reconciliation job has used the same 1ck_ key for two years. It works, nobody has touched it, and there has been no incident.
blocks.question: What is the strongest argument for changing it?

options.text: It has probably been copied somewhere by now, so it should be rotated on principle.
options.feedback: Plausible but unfalsifiable, and it will lose to 'if it isn't broken' every time. It also suggests rotation as the fix when the durable problem is duration itself.

options.text: A credential with no expiry converts any single past leak into permanent access, so the fix is a short-lived token rather than a fresher long-lived one.
options.feedback: Correct, and it is the argument that actually changes the design. Rotation resets the clock; expiry removes the property that makes a leak permanent. Exchange the key for a short-lived JWT at the point of use.

options.text: Two years exceeds most compliance rotation windows, so it is an audit finding.
options.feedback: Often true and useful for getting the work scheduled, but it argues from policy rather than risk, and it is satisfied by rotating to another two-year key.

options.text: The job should use mTLS instead, which does not expire.
options.feedback: Certificates do expire, and swapping the credential type without shortening its life leaves the same standing-access problem in a different format.

quiz.question: What does the audit log use to stay tamper-evident?
quiz.explanation: Audit entries form a SHA-256 hash chain, and inserts go through a SECURITY DEFINER function.

quiz.question: What happens the moment a honeytoken is read?
options: A critical verdict is recorded but the request proceeds
Nothing until a human reviews it
quiz.explanation: The read is allowed to avoid tipping off the attacker, but a critical verdict blocks their next auth.

quiz.question: What does DPoP protect against?
options: Use of a stolen JWT without the matching private key
quiz.explanation: DPoP binds a JWT to a client keypair, so a stolen token is useless without the private key.

title: Human Factor Auth for treasury
summary: Require a password or passkey from a real person before a treasury wallet can send, swap, or export.

blocks.text: Human Factor Auth (HFA, v0.56) puts a person in the loop on the operations that move money. Treasury wallet send, swap, and export can each require a password or a passkey before they proceed: regardless of what token the caller holds.
The policy resolves in a fixed order, most specific first:

items: The user's own human_factor_auth_policies.
Then human_factor_auth on the relevant wallet_spend_policies.
Then the system defaults.

blocks.text: HFA is about proving a human is present. It is deliberately separate from the agent guardrails in the Transactions track, which bound what an agent may attempt in the first place.

steps.text: Read the current policy.
Require a passkey for sends and exports, and a password for swaps.
Clients can prefetch the effective policy so they know which step-up to prompt for before the user hits send.
Satisfy the step-up. Mint a re-auth token, then present it on the protected call.
steps.code:
curl -s -X POST https://api.1claw.co/v1/auth/reauth/begin \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ONECLAW_TOKEN" \
  -d '{"method":"passkey"}'
# complete the ceremony, then send the resulting rat_ token:
#   -H "X-Auth-Confirm: rat_..."

blocks.text: Two webhooks make HFA observable: human_factor_auth.satisfied and human_factor_auth.denied. A run of denials is a strong signal that something is trying to move funds without a human.
Social-login users may have no password. If you require the password method they cannot satisfy it: have them enrol a passkey or TOTP at /settings/security first.

blocks.situation: You set the HFA policy to require a password for treasury sends. A batch of users, all of whom signed up through Google, immediately cannot send at all.
blocks.question: What happened?

options.text: Their sessions predate the policy and need re-issuing.
options.feedback: Policy changes take effect on the next protected call, so a stale session would surface as a prompt rather than an impossibility.

options.text: Social-login users have no password to verify, so the step-up cannot be satisfied at all.
options.feedback: Correct. There is nothing to check, so the requirement is unsatisfiable rather than merely inconvenient. Those users need a passkey or TOTP enrolled, or the policy should require a method they can actually present.

options.text: Google OAuth sessions are not eligible for step-up authentication.
options.feedback: They are eligible; the mechanism works for any authenticated user. The gap is the specific factor you chose, not the login method.

options.text: The policy resolved to the wallet spend policy instead of the user policy.
options.feedback: Resolution runs user policy first, then wallet, then defaults, so the user policy is what applied. It applied correctly and the requirement is the problem.

quiz.question: In what order does an HFA policy resolve?
options: User policy, then wallet spend policy, then defaults
Defaults, then wallet policy, then user policy
quiz.explanation: Resolution runs most specific first: the user's human_factor_auth_policies, then human_factor_auth on the wallet spend policy, then system defaults.

quiz.question: Why prefetch GET /v1/treasury/wallets/auth-policy?
options: So the client knows which step-up to prompt for before the user acts
quiz.explanation: Prefetching the effective policy lets the client show the right passkey or password prompt up front, instead of failing the send and retrying.

quiz.question: A social-login user has no password set. What breaks if the HFA policy requires the password method?
options: Nothing: a password is generated for them
The policy silently falls back to no step-up
They cannot satisfy the step-up until they enrol a passkey or TOTP
quiz.explanation: Without a password there is nothing to verify. They need to enrol a passkey or TOTP at /settings/security, or the policy should require one of those methods instead.

title: OIDC federation and Sign in with 1Claw
summary: Let external systems verify 1Claw-issued JWTs directly, so you can drop static API keys at the boundary.

blocks.text: 1Claw publishes a standard OpenID Connect issuer at https://api.1claw.co. That means an external relying party (Anthropic Workload Identity Federation, GCP STS, AWS STS) can validate a 1Claw-issued token against public keys instead of holding a long-lived shared secret.

items: GET /.well-known/openid-configuration: the issuer metadata.
GET /.well-known/jwks.json: the public signing keys.
Agent JWTs are signed EdDSA; federation tokens are RS256 from an HSM-backed RSA-2048 KMS key.
Each active key version publishes under a deterministic kid: eddsa-vN and rs256-vN.

blocks.text: Federation is deny-by-default. An agent has federation_enabled false until you turn it on, and federation_audiences is an allowlist where empty means deny everything.

steps.text: Read the issuer metadata. No auth required; this is what the relying party fetches.
Enable federation on the agent and allowlist exactly one audience.
Exchange the agent credential for a federated token using RFC 8693 token exchange.
Present the resulting RS256 JWT to the external service, which validates it against the JWKS.

blocks.text: TTL defaults to 900 seconds and is hard-capped at 3600. That cap is the point: a federated token is meant to be short-lived, unlike the static key it replaces.

Separately, 1Claw can act as an OAuth2 authorization server, "Sign in with 1Claw", with PKCE-required authorize, token, and userinfo endpoints under /v1/oauth. That is for signing users into your app, whereas federation is for machine identity at a service boundary.

blocks.situation: A partner wants to call your service using a 1Claw-issued federated token. They ask you to accept any token that validates against the 1Claw JWKS, since that proves it came from 1Claw.
blocks.question: Is that sufficient?

options.text: Yes. A valid signature from the published JWKS is exactly the guarantee federation provides.
options.feedback: It proves the issuer, which is necessary and not sufficient. Any 1Claw customer can mint a validly signed token; without checking who it was minted for, you accept tokens intended for someone else.

options.text: No. You must also validate the audience, or you will accept tokens minted for a different relying party.
options.feedback: Correct, and this is the classic confused-deputy shape. The agent's federation_audiences allowlist controls what it may request; your service must independently check that aud names you.

options.text: No. Federated tokens are RS256 and you should require EdDSA.
options.feedback: Backwards. Agent JWTs are EdDSA; federation tokens are deliberately RS256 because external relying parties overwhelmingly expect RSA. The algorithm is not the gap.

options.text: Yes, provided you pin a single kid from the JWKS.
options.feedback: Pinning a kid breaks silently on key rotation and still does not tell you who the token was issued for. It adds fragility without adding the missing check.

quiz.question: What does OIDC federation let you remove?
options: Static long-lived API keys at the service boundary
quiz.explanation: The relying party validates a short-lived 1Claw-issued JWT against published JWKS, so there is no long-lived shared secret to store or rotate.

quiz.question: An agent has federation_enabled true but federation_audiences empty. What happens?
options: Only the default audience is allowed
The agent cannot authenticate at all
quiz.explanation: federation_audiences is an allowlist and empty means deny all. Federation is deny-by-default throughout.

quiz.question: Which algorithms sign agent JWTs and federation tokens?
options: EdDSA for agent JWTs, RS256 for federation tokens
quiz.explanation: Agent JWTs use the EC_SIGN_ED25519 key (EdDSA); federation tokens use an HSM-backed RSA-2048 key (RS256), because external relying parties overwhelmingly expect RSA.

concepts.note: JWKS, audience binding, and short expiry
